item.title: California Ticket Resale Cap Bill Fails to Move Forward
item.description:
[Intro music plays]
Host: Welcome to our podcast, where we dive into the latest news and trends in the entertainment industry. Today, we're talking about the recent development in California's ticketing bill, AB 1720. I'm your host, [Name], and let's get started.
[Soft music plays in the background]
Host: So, what's the news? California's most comprehensive ticketing bill to date, AB 1720, has failed to move forward in the state's Senate Appropriations Committee. The bill, introduced by state assembly member Matt Haney, aimed to make it illegal to resell tickets to live events at more than 10% above face value.
[Short pause]
Host: Haney stated that the bill would have helped remove the incentives that fuel predatory ticket resale, while still allowing fans to resell their tickets and recover their costs. He expressed disappointment that the bill didn't advance, but emphasized that it doesn't change the reality that fans, artists, and venues are losing out to middlemen who extract more and more profit.
[Soft music continues]
Host: The bill faced significant opposition from secondary ticketing companies like StubHub, which spent $3.4 million lobbying against the legislation. StubHub argues that they provide a secure marketplace for fans to access live events, and that more choice and flexibility put fans first.
[Short pause]
Host: On the other hand, the bill was backed by organizations like the National Independent Venue Association and the Music Artists Coalition. They believe that capping resale ticket prices would help fans, artists, and venues, rather than profiteers.
[Music transitions to a slightly more upbeat tone]
Host: While the original bill had broader implications, it was later amended to only apply to independent venues with a capacity of 3,000 or fewer. This means that larger arena and stadium shows would not have been affected.
[Short pause]
Host: As Haney pointed out, the current system can be frustrating for fans, with professional brokers and bots buying up tickets and reselling them at inflated prices. The markup from these resales doesn't support the artists, venues, or staff who make live events possible.
[Outro music plays]
Host: That's all for today. The fate of AB 1720 may be decided, but the conversation about ticketing reform is far from over. Thanks for tuning in, and we'll catch you in the next episode.
[Outro music continues to play until the end]
